## merge vs rebase

**merge** — join two branches, keep full history. Creates merge commit.

```
A---B---C  main
     \
      D---E  feature
           \
            M  ← merge commit (has 2 parents)
```

**rebase** — replay feature commits on top of target. Linear history, no merge commit.

```
A---B---C  main
             \
              D'--E'  ← rebased (new commits, same changes)
```

---

## when use what

**merge when:**
- public/shared branch (never rebase these)
- want preserve exact history + context
- merging main → long-lived feature (safe catch-up)
- team prefers non-destructive ops

**rebase when:**
- cleaning local feature branch before PR
- want linear, readable history
- squashing WIP commits
- solo branch, not pushed yet

---

## tradeoffs

| | merge | rebase |
|---|---|---|
| history | true, messy | clean, rewritten |
| conflicts | once | per commit replayed |
| safety | always safe | dangerous on shared branches |
| bisect/blame | harder | easier |
| context | preserves "when" | loses "when" |

---

## golden rule

> **Never rebase commits already pushed to shared branch.**

Rebase rewrites commit hashes. Others have old hashes → chaos.

---

## common pattern

```bash
# keep feature branch current (safe)
git checkout feature
git rebase main        # clean, linear

# merge to main when done
git checkout main
git merge feature      # fast-forward, no merge commit needed
```

Conflict mid-rebase → fix → `git rebase --continue`. Bail → `git rebase --abort`.
